Can someone please explain the significance of this in simpler, easier to process terms?

One view of statistics is that it consists of good strategies for estimating hidden parameters or hidden models given noisy observations. If you know that the hidden information was generated at random, and you know the probabilities involved, then Bayesian statistics is provably optimal for solving the problem of estimating the hidden information. The catch is that in most real world applications of statistics the hidden information is not generated at random according to known distributions. Furthermore, if you assume that your hidden information was generated by one distribution and it was in fact generated by a different one, then your warranty is void and your estimates won't be as accurate as you think they are. (Non-Bayesians/frequentists attempt to avoid this problem by answering a slightly different question - arguably one which is unnatural and easy to misinterpret).

For cases where nothing is known about the means of generation of the hidden parameters Bayesian statisticians have attempted to agree on so-called uninformative priors - all-purpose assumptions about how the hidden data was generated - but there are various examples which show that these can have unattractive properties in some situations, which, IMHO, are reflections of the fact that assuming that your hidden information was generated in a way which it was not will lead you to wrong answers. This paper seems to be attempting to justify another way to select uninformative priors - agreed assumptions for how the hidden data was generated.

Note that some Bayesian statisticians believe that, in practice, you are very likely to have enough information to make at least some sort of guess about how that hidden data was generated, or at least what it is likely to look like - see e.g. the discussion at http://andrewgelman.com/2014/11/21/youre-using-proper-informative-prior-youre-leaving-money-table/.
